evidenced by the recent speech given by the country’s SAC Commander, Min Aung Hlaing. At large, the international community must respond, and this is where the Myanmar Tribunal will play a critical role. As noted by Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, Yang Jiechi in the UN’s report, there is increasing concern over the “tendency of the civilian dispensation...to modify, amend or even nullify failures reports of the UN Human Rights Council.” The Tribunal will ensure accountability, particularly in Myanmar, which is still working to put the horror of genocide on trial.
In April, just prior to the release of the UN Report on Myanmar, Henri Tiphagne, the executive director of the Serious Organized Crime Research Centre (SOCRCRE) and a member of the UN Sanctions Committee's Panel of Experts on Myanmar, reached out to the director of the Permanent Mission of Myanmar to the UN, Kyaw Moe Tun, to explore a potential collaboration between the SOCRCRE and the Permanent Mission. This meeting became possible since the Permanent Mission knew about a precedent from the Panel’s work during its “703 Mission to Myanmar in February 2018” on “chapter VI or is there a way you could valorise what I propose here”. A letter drafted following the meeting details how SOCRCRE and the Permanent Mission can cooperate and collaborate, specifying what, how, and where. This kind of collaboration between the UN, Myanmar, and civil society is greatly needed to ensure accountability, peace, and stability for the population.
